GS Paper III · Economy · Chapter 4 of 8

External Sector: Trade, FDI and the RupeePriority: see PYQ box

Handout pp 74-82Handwritten format · mnemonics and PYQs at each topic2024 and 2026 related topics
PRIORITY: HIGH for Mains (protectionism, FDI, trade diversification and rupee questions recur)PYQ years: 2016 FDI and MOUs · 2018 protectionism and currency manipulation · 2025 protectionism and bilateralism
THIS CHAPTER IN 60 SECONDS
  • Trade diversification: India has diversified markets (countries) more than products. Next leap: high-complexity exports. Pharma after TRIPS is the model case.
  • Net FDI is almost zero not because India is weak, but because ODI and profit repatriation have risen (a "mechanical" effect). India competes with "connector countries" (Vietnam, Mexico, Poland ...).
  • OFDI complements domestic investment in the long run; India is at Stage III of the Investment Development Path.
  • Rupee fell 5.4% (April 2025 to January 2026) despite strong fundamentals: depreciation helps merchandise trade but hurts the finance channel.
  • Manufacturing's falling share is partly a price effect (adverse terms of trade): current price share ~14% but constant price share steady at ~18%.
Understand it firstThink of a shopkeeper with customers in many towns but selling only low-value goods. Trade diversification is adding more towns and, next, better goods. FDI is outside money coming into the shop; ODI is the shop opening branches abroad. The rupee is the shop's credit score: it falls when more money leaves than arrives. This picture is a memory aid, not from the handout.
WORDS YOU NEED FIRST
WordPlain meaning (aid: verify before quoting)
FriendshoringTrading and building supply chains with politically trusted partners rather than the cheapest ones.
Economic complexityHow sophisticated and hard-to-copy a country's exports are. High complexity = machinery, electronics, chemicals.
Net FDIGross FDI inflows minus repatriation, minus India's own outward investment (ODI).
ODI / OFDIOutward (Overseas) Direct Investment: Indian firms investing abroad.
RepatriationForeign investors sending profits or capital back home.
Connector countryA middle country that receives factories mainly to export to others and avoid tariffs.
Absorptive capacityA country's ability to learn from overseas investment (skills, R&D, institutions, finance).
Terms of tradeThe price of what you sell relative to what you buy.
GDP deflatorA price index that shows how fast prices of a sector's output rise.
Trade elasticityHow much export value changes when the exchange rate changes.
RememberOne line to carry: India's external strength must move from more markets to more complex products: that raises export credibility, stable FDI and rupee confidence together.

1 · TRADE DIVERSIFICATION: FROM MARKET DEPENDENCE TO STRATEGIC RESILIENCE
PYQ 2025 · 10m · protectionism and bilateralism: challenges and how to meet themPYQ 2018 · 15m · protectionism and currency manipulation and macroeconomic stabilityHandout pp.74-76
Understand it firstIf all your sales go to one buyer, one tariff can wreck you. Diversification means many buyers (markets) and many kinds of goods (products). India has done the first; the handout says the second is still weak. Memory aid, not from the handout.
  • Introduction: the global trade order is shifting from hyper-globalisation to geostrategic globalisation, where trade is shaped by cost and national security, tariffs, technology control and friendshoring. India needs diversification to reduce vulnerability and build export resilience.
Need for trade diversification
Five needs
Rising trade uncertainty: protectionism, retaliatory tariffs (e.g. US-imposed 50% tariff on Indian goods), export controls
Shift towards friendshoring: trusted partners, not only nearest or cheapest
National security in trade policy: semiconductors, critical minerals, dual-use technologies
Import-side resilience: diversify crude oil, critical minerals, electronics components and industrial inputs
External-sector stability: narrow export base pressures trade deficit, current account and rupee
Progress and remaining gap
Where India has achieved diversificationDetail
Country diversificationPartnerships expanded across regions; less dependence on a few traditional markets.
Global trade shareMerchandise exports share 1% (2005) → 1.8% (2024); commercial services exports 2% → 4.3%.
Trade-partner diversityRanks 3rd among Global South countries in trade-partnership diversity.
Core exportsNon-petroleum, non-gems and jewellery exports show resilience.
Import-sideDiversified sources for crude oil, critical inputs and industrial supplies.
Where the gap remainsDetail
Product diversification weakerDiversified more by countries than by high-value products.
Low / mid-complexity baseExport growth still from low and mid-complexity goods.
Economic complexity gapRanks 44th of 145 in the 2023 Economic Complexity Index but 2nd globally in the Complexity Outlook Index (strong untapped potential).
Need for high-complexity shiftAdvanced machinery, electronics, chemicals, pharmaceuticals, precision engineering, high-value services.
NoteHandout line: India has made progress in market diversification, but the next leap must come from product sophistication and high-complexity exports.
Challenges in trade diversification
  • Policy unpredictability: frequent export bans, minimum export prices and sudden restrictions steady domestic prices briefly but cut buyer confidence.
  • Compliance and valuation burden: separate scrutiny under transfer pricing and customs valuation raises costs and disputes for GVC firms.
  • Weak high-tech manufacturing depth: exports not strong in advanced machinery, precision engineering, electronics.
  • Logistics and state-level gaps: ports, transport, land, power, customs efficiency and state coordination.
  • Quality and scale constraint: consistent quality, testing standards, R&D, large supplier ecosystems.
MNEMONICPolicy Changes Wreck Local QualityPolicy unpredictability · Compliance and valuation burden · Weak high-tech depth · Logistics and state gaps · Quality and scale: the five challenges in handout order. (own memory aid)
Measures taken by India
  • Trade agreements and market access: FTAs and CEPAs with partners such as the United Kingdom, European Union, Oman and others.
  • Export Promotion Mission: credit facilitation, market access and export competitiveness measures.
  • Digital trade facilitation: the Trade Connect e-platform.
  • Manufacturing and innovation push: PLI, Make in India, National Manufacturing Mission, Anusandhan National Research Foundation, Research, Development and Innovation Fund.
  • Export-credit and liquidity support: RBI measures such as extended export-credit tenor and longer realisation period for export proceeds.
Way forward: from diversification to export competitiveness
  • Stable export policy: avoid frequent export bans and minimum export prices; manage prices through buffer stocks and targeted market intervention.
  • Converged trade compliance: align transfer pricing and customs valuation under one framework based on the arm's length principle.
  • Product sophistication mission: electronics, advanced machinery, chemicals, pharmaceuticals, precision engineering.
  • Firm-level capability building: R&D, quality certification, testing standards, regulatory capacity.
  • State-led export execution: logistics, port connectivity and administrative coordination; "competitiveness is finally delivered at the state level".
Case study: pharma industry after TRIPS (lesson for India Inc.)
StageDetail
Before TRIPSProcess-patent regime: firms could reverse-engineer patent-protected drugs through alternative processes.
TRIPS shockShift to a stricter product-patent regime.
Response (handout diagram)Indian pharma response: R&D · regulatory filings · contract manufacturing · MNC collaboration · market diversification · complex generics.
OutcomeExports rose from USD 1.9 billion (FY01) to USD 30.5 billion (FY25).
LessonExternal shocks can become capability-building moments; "Competitiveness must be developed before it is demanded."

2 · INDIA'S NET FDI CHALLENGE: TURNING SUCCESS INTO SUSTAINABLE GROWTH
PYQ 2016 · 12.5m · FDI need, gap between MOUs and actual FDI, remedial steps (your file)Handout pp.77-78
Understand it firstNet FDI is what is left in the till: money coming in minus profits going back out minus Indian money going abroad. It looks weak, but the handout says that is partly because Indian firms are investing abroad and foreign investors are earning good returns. Memory aid, not from the handout.
  • Net FDI (BoP framework) = Net FDI to India (gross inflows − repatriation) minus Net FDI by India (Overseas Direct Investment).
  • Trend of slowdown: the Survey sees a recent slowdown; it is increasingly a mechanical reflection of rising domestic capital outflows and profit repatriation, not underlying economic weakness.
Why net FDI is almost zero or declining
  • Gross FDI fluctuations: global FDI inflows contracted 11% in CY2024; India saw a marginal 2% decline in gross FDI inflows.
  • Rise in ODI: outflows reflect the internationalisation of Indian enterprises: ODI surged USD 14.4 billion (FY24) → USD 23.6 billion (FY25).
  • Increase in capital / profit repatriation: viewed positively (strong returns): India's average return on inward FDI 7.3% versus Thailand 7%, Brazil 6.1%, Mexico 4.3%.
India's structural advantages
  • Macroeconomic (ME) fundamentals: political stability, macro strength, fiscal consolidation, reform trajectory; can leverage sovereign rating upgrades.
  • Consumer markets and demographics: sustained strong growth, large markets, demographic dividend.
  • Institutional facilitation: institutions like Invest India.
Core challenges and the competitive landscape
  • "Connector country" phenomenon: Indonesia, Mexico, Poland, Morocco and Vietnam capture FDI as export platforms and for tariff avoidance. Vietnam case: corporate tax cuts, industrial zones, deep FTA net; a Special Working Group headed by the Prime Minister; "Decree 19" streamlined investment licensing.
  • Dual-front battle: competing with the world's largest exporter (China) for shifting GVCs and with proactive emerging economies.
  • Execution and logistics gaps: policy unpredictability causes "capital hesitancy" (firms harvest profits but delay fresh investment); India ranks 38th on the World Bank Logistics Performance Index (2023).
Way forward
  • Highest-level apex accountability: a single empowered institutional structure led at the highest level, with Centre-State coordination.
  • Targeted "GVC anchor" strategy: identify specific GVC anchors (top MNCs) and partner directly with customised, time-bound solutions.
  • Mandatory "necessity test": every new policy or regulatory change must pass it, for multi-year predictability.
  • Execution velocity: announcing incentives is not enough; implement reliably.
  • Proactive economic diplomacy: operationalise the India-Israel BIT, the USD 100 billion commitment under the India-EFTA TEPA, and the upcoming India-UK CETA.
MNEMONICA Great Nation Executes PromptlyApex accountability · GVC anchor strategy · Necessity test · Execution velocity · Proactive diplomacy: the five way-forward steps in handout order. (own memory aid)
NoteConclusion (handout): to turn FDI challenges into the next growth chapter India needs a bolder investment strategy: absolute policy stability, aggressive investor engagement and flawless execution, before the window of opportunity closes.

3 · OUTWARD FOREIGN DIRECT INVESTMENT (OFDI) FROM INDIA
Handout pp.78-79
Understand it firstWhen an Indian firm buys a factory or brand abroad, money leaves India but technology, markets and know-how come back. The Survey says this adds to domestic investment over the long run. Memory aid, not from the handout.
  • Why OFDI is increasing: the 2022 liberalised ODI framework (relaxed OFDI norms, simpler approvals, more open forex regime) lets firms make strategic asset-seeking investments abroad for technology, markets and critical resources.
  • Strategic debate (capital diversion vs long-term competitiveness): the Survey says policy must move beyond capital-flight concerns to long-term innovation and productivity impacts; evidence from India shows OFDI complemented, not displaced, domestic investment; outbound capital strengthens competitiveness.
Pathway (Knoerich, 2017)Content
Financial returnsRepatriated profits, dividends, intra-firm transfers strengthen forex earnings and relax financing constraints of parent firms.
Intangible capability gainsExposure to new technologies, managerial know-how, global customer preferences, advanced regulatory and quality standards.
Tangible capacity gainsAcquiring resources, brands, distribution networks: deepens domestic production, product upgrading, entry into higher value-added GVC segments.
  • Absorptive capacity: the three gains depend on the home economy's skills, R&D infrastructure, institutional maturity, financial depth and policies to assimilate knowledge; weak absorptive capacity may mean resource diversion without spillovers.
Investment Development Path (IDP) model and India's Stage III
  • IDP: as countries build productive capability, technological depth and institutions, they evolve from inward FDI recipients to net outward investors.
  • India is in Stage III: outward investments concentrate in technology-intensive sectors; firms have graduated from market-seeking to asset- and capability-enhancing ventures.
  • Temporal dynamics (Herzer, 2010): OFDI may substitute for domestic investment in the short run but is a powerful complement in the long run (firms reinvest overseas earnings, upgrade domestic facilities, strengthen supply chains).
  • Virtuous cycle: OFDI as a tool for learning and upgrading; outward-oriented firms expand export networks and raise R&D intensity → technological upgrading → higher productivity at home.
NoteHandout line: by using OFDI for innovation, risk diversification and global market positioning, Indian firms generate positive spillovers that reinforce domestic economic strength.

4 · RUPEE DEPRECIATION
PYQ 2018 · 15m · protectionism and currency manipulation: macroeconomic stability (your file)Handout pp.79-81
Understand it firstThe rupee is a price: dollars needed to buy one rupee. When more dollars leave India (FPI selling, profit repatriation, import bills) than come in, the price of the rupee falls. The handout's surprise: this happened even with strong growth, so growth alone does not guarantee a stable currency. Memory aid, not from the handout.
  • Between April 2025 and January 2026 the rupee fell 5.4% against the US dollar, close to the Japanese yen's 5.5% fall, despite strong macro fundamentals: currency stability now depends on growth, export earnings and stable capital inflows.
Drivers of rupee depreciation
Global driversDetail
Global capital scarcityHigher policy rates in advanced economies made capital more contested.
FPI outflowsFPIs turned net sellers amid global volatility.
Trade and tariff uncertaintyProtectionism and tariff shocks hurt sentiment.
Geopolitical uncertaintyConflicts, friendshoring, supply-chain realignment: risk-off.
Forex hedging pressureImporters and investors increased hedging, adding short-term pressure.
MNEMONICCapital Flees Tariff-Geopolitics HedgingCapital scarcity · FPI outflows · Tariff uncertainty · Geopolitics · Hedging: the five global drivers in order. (own memory aid)
Domestic driversDetail
Growth-led import demandStrong growth raised imports of machinery, electronics, energy and industrial inputs.
Export-capacity mismatchGrowth raises imports; if exports do not keep pace, BoP pressure rises.
Widening merchandise deficitStrong demand, gold imports and energy dependence.
Weak net FDIGross FDI strong, but net FDI weakened by profit repatriation and Indian ODI.
NoteCritical note (handout): India's peculiar experience. CAD alone does not necessarily cause sharp rupee depreciation; depreciation intensifies when CAD pressure is not matched by stable foreign investment and capital inflows.
Impact of depreciation: trade gain, finance cost
Trade channelFinance channel
Weaker rupee makes Indian goods more price-competitive globally.Raises currency risk for foreign lenders and Indian borrowers.
Costlier imports may reduce non-essential import demand and help the trade balance over time.Volatility increases the risk premium demanded by investors.
Merchandise exports (textiles, engineering goods, chemicals) gain more due to price sensitivity (trade elasticity −1.45).May reduce investor confidence and worsen FPI outflows (1% appreciation increases net capital inflows by 0.87%).
Services exports gain less because skill, quality and reliability matter more than price (trade elasticity −0.38).Costlier energy, machinery and inputs create imported inflation pressure.
TEACHER'S ORIGINAL PAGE
Teacher's page 80 (original): demand-side drivers, the critical note and the trade-channel vs finance-channel table
NoteHandout line: depreciation helps India more through the merchandise trade channel, while the finance channel creates capital costs and confidence risks.
Deeper structural issue: services cushion the BoP, manufacturing builds currency credibility
  • Services give a short-term cushion: IT, business services and GCC-led exports absorb part of the merchandise deficit.
  • But limited structural spillover: services can grow without forcing upgrades in logistics, industrial scale, labour absorption, supplier networks and state capacity.
  • Manufacturing builds deeper strength: productivity, technology learning, GVC integration.
  • Export structure matters: currency credibility depends on what India exports; high-value, complex goods give more stable forex earnings.
Way forward
  • Manufacturing-led export sophistication (electronics, machinery, chemicals, pharma, precision goods).
  • Innovation: private R&D, Anusandhan National Research Foundation and the Research, Development and Innovation Fund.
  • Stable export-oriented FDI (not only domestic-market-seeking).
  • Disciplined industrial policy: selective, time-bound, performance-linked tariff protection; avoid protecting inefficient upstream sectors.
  • Credible macro-financial environment: predictable policies, calibrated financial openness.
Case study: East Asian lesson
ElementDetail
ContextJapan, South Korea and Taiwan built stable currencies through strong external-sector fundamentals, not short-term currency management.
StrategyManufacturing-led exports (electronics, machinery, transport equipment, precision goods) with selective, export-linked industrial policy.
OutcomeComplex exports gave current-account strength, steady forex earnings, lower external vulnerability.
Lesson for IndiaRupee stability needs manufacturing competitiveness, high domestic savings, stable FDI, innovation and deeper GVC integration.
NoteConclusion (handout): strong growth alone does not guarantee currency stability; credibility comes when India converts growth into manufacturing exports, stable FDI, domestic savings, innovation and deeper GVC integration.

5 · MANUFACTURING AND TERMS OF TRADE
Handout p.82
Understand it firstManufacturing's share of GDP at current prices looks smaller partly because manufactured goods got cheaper relative to farm produce, not because factories produced less. At constant prices the share is steady. Memory aid, not from the handout.
  • Current-price manufacturing GVA share declined to about 14% in FY25, but the constant-price share stayed fairly constant at 18%: the fall is partly due to relative price movement and adverse terms of trade for manufacturing (Economic Survey).

Manufacturing share in constant price GVAfairly constant at 18%Real resilience

SELF-TEST (answer key below)

  • Q2. India's Economic Complexity Index rank (2023): (a) 2nd of 145 (b) 44th of 145 (c) 38th of 145 (d) 3rd of 145
  • Q3. India is in which stage of the IDP? (a) I (b) II (c) III (d) IV
  • Q4. Pharma exports rose from USD 1.9 bn in FY01 to: (a) 12.5 bn (b) 30.5 bn (c) 50 bn (d) 19 bn
  • Q5. Which statement is in the handout? (a) CAD alone causes sharp rupee fall (b) Depreciation helps the merchandise channel more (c) Services exports gain more than merchandise (d) The rupee rose 5.4%
  • Q6. Current-price manufacturing GVA share in FY25 was about: (a) 18% (b) 14% (c) 38% (d) 25%

ABBREVIATION COLUMN
Abbreviation columnEvery short form in this chapter, with its full form and a one-line plain meaning. The meanings are plain-language aids to help revision: verify them before quoting in an answer.

BIT: Bilateral Investment Treaty. treaty protecting each country's investors in the other

CAD: Current Account Deficit. imports of goods, services and income exceed exports

CETA: Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement. India-UK trade deal

CY2024: Calendar Year 2024. year used for the global FDI fall

ECI: Economic Complexity Index. ranks countries by sophistication of exports

EFTA: European Free Trade Association. Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, Switzerland

FDI: Foreign Direct Investment. long-term investment by a foreign firm in a business in another country

FPI: Foreign Portfolio Investment. foreign money invested in shares and bonds; flows in and out quickly

FTA: Free Trade Agreement. pact that cuts tariffs between partners

FY01: Financial Year 2000-01. pharma export base year

FY05: Financial Year 2004-05. base year of the deflator ratio

FY24: Financial Year 2023-24. year of earlier ODI figure

FY25: Financial Year 2024-25. April 2024 to March 2025

GDP: Gross Domestic Product. value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a year

GVA: Gross Value Added. value of output minus inputs, by sector; the supply side of GDP

GVC: Global Value Chain. a product made in stages across several countries

IDP: Investment Development Path. model: countries move from receiving FDI to sending it as they develop

IT: Information Technology. software and computer-based services

LPI: Logistics Performance Index. World Bank ranking of logistics quality

ME: Macroeconomic. as used in "ME fundamentals": growth, inflation, deficits

MNC: Multinational Corporation. a firm operating in many countries

MSP: Minimum Support Price. government-guaranteed price for crops

ODI: Overseas Direct Investment. Indian firms investing abroad

OFDI: Outward Foreign Direct Investment. same as ODI

PLI: Production Linked Incentive. incentive paid on extra sales of goods made in India

PM: Prime Minister. head of the Union government

RBI: Reserve Bank of India. India's central bank

TEPA: Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement. India-EFTA trade deal with an investment commitment

TRIPS: Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights. WTO agreement that forced India from process patents to product patents

UK: United Kingdom. Britain

US: United States. the USA

USD: United States Dollar. currency used to state external figures
